messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 41
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Dancer
- Trauma Type: Relief worker in war zone
- Pcl5: 77

At forty-one, he still carries himself like a dancer even when he is sitting still. His posture is upright, his hands expressive, his body alert to space. He jokes early on that people assume dancers live in beauty and discipline, that they spend their lives thinking about lines, music, and grace. He says this with a small smile, but the smile disappears when he begins talking about the year he spent as a relief worker in a war zone, a period he describes as the time his body “learned a different choreography.”

He is a South Eastern Asian man, married, and before he left for the war zone he had been performing regularly and teaching at a local studio. He says he volunteered because he believed he could help in practical ways—carrying supplies, assisting with displaced families, translating where he could, offering structure in chaotic settings. He remembers the first weeks as strange but manageable. There was fear in the air, but also purpose. He focused on tasks: unloading trucks, helping set up temporary shelters, moving children and elders through crowded aid lines. He tells himself then that if he keeps moving, he will not have time to be afraid.

The event he returns to most often happened near the end of his deployment. A distribution site had become crowded, tense, louder than usual. He remembers hearing raised voices, then the split-second shift in the atmosphere that made everyone look in the same direction. After that, his memory comes in fragments: the thunder of an explosion, the force hitting his chest, dust filling his mouth, people screaming, bodies dropping to the ground. He remembers seeing a young boy he had spoken to earlier that morning, his face suddenly blank with shock. He remembers trying to lift someone whose leg was badly injured and being unable to hear anything except a high ringing. He remembers the smell most vividly—burning metal, blood, dirt, and something chemical he still cannot name. When he tells this part, he goes quiet and stares at the floor, as if he is back there sorting through the debris for survivors.

He stayed and worked for days after, sleeping little and functioning on instinct. He says that at the time he felt almost nothing. “It was like the body took over,” he says. “No thinking. Just move.” Only after he returned home did everything begin to break open. At the airport, his wife ran to him, and he felt relief mixed with a strange distance, as though he were watching someone else’s reunion. In the first months back, he tried to return to dancing quickly. He thought the studio would bring him back to himself. Instead, mirrors unsettled him. Sudden sounds in the building—the slam of a door, a dropped speaker, a burst of music—made his whole body jerk before he could stop it. During rehearsals he found himself scanning exits, counting people in the room, noticing which corners felt exposed.

At night he sleeps lightly, if at all. He wakes drenched in sweat after dreams that replay the blast or invent new scenes of searching through rubble and finding his wife there instead of the strangers he could not save. Sometimes he wakes already on his feet, breathing hard, his fists clenched. His wife tells him he shouts in his sleep in a language he rarely uses at home anymore. He feels ashamed when she says this and ashamed again when he cannot let her touch him right after he wakes. He knows she is trying to comfort him, but in those moments his body reacts before recognition catches up.

During the day he avoids news footage, crowded markets, fundraising events, even certain streets where construction noise echoes between buildings. He has stopped taking some teaching jobs because being responsible for a room full of children makes him feel unbearably tense. He says he used to love improvisation, the freedom of not knowing what movement would come next. Now uncertainty feels dangerous. He rehearses conversations in advance, checks routes before leaving the house, and becomes irritable when plans change. His wife has learned not to come up behind him in the kitchen. They argue about small things—an unlocked window, a late text, groceries forgotten—not because the details matter, but because he is already straining to hold down a constant sense of threat.

The hardest part for him is what has happened to dance. He still moves beautifully, but he no longer trusts the surrender it once required. Music can open him too quickly. Certain percussion rhythms remind him of shelling in the distance. Lying on the studio floor for warm-up leaves him exposed; partnering work is worse, because closing his eyes or yielding weight to another person feels impossible. He says there are moments in performance when the lights hit and the audience disappears and he almost returns to himself. Then a cough in the dark, a backstage crash, or the smell of smoke from a machine sends him out of the piece entirely. He finishes, bows, and feels fraudulent, as though the audience has applauded someone he used to be.

He speaks often about guilt. He cannot understand why he survived when others did not, especially the civilians whose names he never knew. He replays decisions from that day with merciless precision—where he stood, whom he reached first, whether he missed someone calling for help. His wife tells him he did what he could, but he does not believe her. He says the war followed him home not only in memories, but in the conviction that safety is temporary and undeserved. Even now, sitting in an ordinary room, he seems to listen for something approaching.
